extracted.intended_audience: readers of satirical 19th-century fiction / students of social satire
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Samuel Butler's Erewhon (a 19th-century satirical novel) describing inverted social, medical, and legal norms in the fictional country; useful for analysis of satire, social critique, and fictional institutional rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ill health tried before a jury
rubrics_metrics.description: In that country if a man falls into ill health, or catches any disorder, or fails bodily in any way before he is seventy years old, he is tried before a jury of his countrymen, and if convicted is held up to public scorn and sentenced more or less severely as the case may be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage explains this as a general legal principle: physical ailments (before age seventy) are treated as matters for criminal/judicial determination rather than purely medical care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivision of illnesses into crimes and misdemeanours
rubrics_metrics.description: There are subdivisions of illnesses into crimes and misdemeanours as with offences amongst ourselves—a man being punished very heavily for serious illness, while failure of eyes or hearing in one over sixty-five, who has had good health hitherto, is dealt with by fine only, or imprisonment in default of payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severity of sanction depends on classification; age and prior health affect penalties (e.g., sensory failure in the elderly treated less harshly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal acts treated as moral ailments (medicalised criminals)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a man forges a cheque, or sets his house on fire, or robs with violence from the person ... he is either taken to a hospital and most carefully tended at the public expense, or if he is in good circumstances, he lets it be known to all his friends that he is suffering from a severe fit of immorality, just as we do when we are ill, and they come and visit him with great solicitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal behaviour is conceptualised as a moral/medical condition; wealthy offenders may advertise their 'fit of immorality' to obtain sympathetic treatment; the social response resembles medical caregiving rather than punitive ostracism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misfortune and ill luck as social offences
rubrics_metrics.description: Ill luck of any kind, or even ill treatment at the hands of others, is considered an offence against society, inasmuch as it makes people uncomfortable to hear of it. Loss of fortune, therefore, or loss of some dear friend on whom another was much dependent, is punished hardly less severely than physical delinquency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-fault misfortunes (bereavement, loss) are legally and socially regulated and punished because they disturb social comfort; this inverts common sympathy norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etiquette forbids commonplace health-compliments
rubrics_metrics.description: All the ordinary greetings among ourselves, such as, How do you do? and the like, are considered signs of gross ill-breeding; nor do the politer classes tolerate even such a common complimentary remark as telling a man that he is looking well. They salute each other with, 'I hope you are good this morning;’ or 'I hope you have recovered from the snappishness from which you were suffering when I last saw you.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social protocol requires addressing moral status rather than physical appearance; greeting formulas reflect emphasis on moral condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role, status, and authority of straighteners
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a class of men trained in soul-craft, whom they call straighteners ... These men practise much as medical men in England, and receive a quasi-surreptitious fee on every visit. They are treated with the same unreserve, and obeyed as readily, as our own doctors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Straighteners are the institutional experts on moral maladies: they diagnose, prescribe, and command social deference analogous to physicians; their authority underpins legal/medical practice in Erewhon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted treatments and sanctions by straighteners
rubrics_metrics.description: Though his remedies are sometimes exceedingly painful, involving close confinement for weeks, and in some cases the most cruel physical tortures ... So the Erewhonians take a flogging once a week, and a diet of bread and water for two or three months together, whenever their straightener recommends it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepted therapeutic regimen for moral ailments includes corporal punishment, prolonged dietary restriction, and confinement; such practices are socially accepted as curative rather than purely punitive. Example prescriptions (case-specific) include fines double the embezzled money, bread and milk for six months, and severe monthly flogging for twelve months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of patient compliance and legal enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: I never heard of a reasonable Erewhonian refusing to do what his straightener told him, any more than of a reasonable Englishman refusing to undergo even the most frightful operation, if his doctors told him it was necessary. ... the sanitary laws of Erewhon are very rigorous, and unless the straightener was satisfied that his orders had been obeyed, the patient would have been taken to a hospital (as the poor are).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance with straightener orders is socially normative and backed by law; refusal can result in hospitalization and worse treatment under sanitary statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment of physical illness vs openness about moral disease
rubrics_metrics.description: They conceal ill health by every cunning and hypocrisy and artifice which they can devise, they are quite open about the most flagrant mental diseases ... For they regard bodily ailments as the more venial in proportion as they have been produced by causes independent of the constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social strategy: hide physical sickness to avoid stigma; be candid about moral failings which are treated and displayed differently. The society values appearance of bodily robustness while treating moral deficits publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training regimen for straighteners (practical vice-experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: The student for the profession of straightener is required to set apart certain seasons for the practice of each vice in turn, as a religious duty. These seasons are called 'fasts,' and are continued by the student until he finds that he really can subdue all the more usual vices in his own person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional qualification requires experiential immersion in vices (fasts), with specialists focusing on branches; some practitioners reportedly die in the course of such study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal Bereavement Court treats bereavement as offence
rubrics_metrics.description: In Erewhon as in other countries there are some courts of justice that deal with special subjects. Misfortune generally ... admits of classification, and a court is assigned to each of the main heads ... I strolled into the Personal Bereavement Court, and was much both interested and pained by listening to the trial of a man who was accused of having just lost a wife ... The jury returned a verdict of guilty ... The judge ... commuted sentence to one of three months, with the option of a fine of twenty-five per cent. of the money you have received from the insurance company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bereavement is legally adjudicated; courts assign guilt and penalties; mitigation (e.g., insurance) may alter sentence but the baseline presumes wrongdoing in being unlucky.

rubrics_metrics.name: No excuse for youth, inexperience, or intimidation
rubrics_metrics.description: The lad ... pleaded that he was young, inexperienced, greatly in awe of his guardian ... 'Young man,' said the judge sternly, 'do not talk nonsense. People have no right to be young, inexperienced, greatly in awe of their guardians, and without independent professional advice. If by such indiscretions they outrage the moral sense of their friends, they must expect to suffer accordingly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal standard rejects personal vulnerability or naivety as exculpatory; defendants are expected to have no right to such conditions and are punished for resulting moral/social failings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disease (e.g., consumption) criminalised; sentencing based on social danger
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulmonary consumption—an offence which was punished with death until quite recently ... The judge emphasised prior convictions/incidents, dismissed origin excuses (parentage, accidents), and sentenced the prisoner to imprisonment with hard labour for life; the court also may prescribe one of three official remedies (e.g., two tablespoonfuls of castor oil daily).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being diseased is framed as moral/constitutional fault irrespective of cause; sentencing considers past record and perceived social danger (including fear of empowering physicians), and may include life sentences and ritual 'remedies' ordered at conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court procedure modeled on European practice but reframed ideologically
rubrics_metrics.description: The prisoner was placed in the dock, and the jury were sworn much as in Europe; almost all our own modes of procedure were reproduced, even to the requiring the prisoner to plead guilty or not guilty. Counsel for the prisoner was allowed to urge everything that could be said in his defence ... The summing up of the judge was admirable ... the trial was absolutely impartial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal procedural elements (jury, plea, counsel, summing-up) exist, but judicial rhetoric and ideological framing (disease as guilt, social policy) determine substantive outcomes; impartiality claimed, but social axioms shape sentences.
